title: Who should not take a river cruise
subtitle: And who, having done one properly, won't go back to an ocean ship.

text: Both formats are right. Neither is right for everyone.
sub: I have talked people out of a river week and out of an ocean week in the same afternoon. The mistake is assuming the word cruise describes one kind of holiday.

title: Four travellers I steer away from a river

items.head: The sea-day loyalist
items.body: No day off, no lounger afternoon, no long empty passage. The pace simply never lets up.

items.head: The family of six
items.body: One dining room and one lounge cannot serve six ages at once. An ocean ship can.

items.head: The space buyer
items.body: Locks cap the dimensions of the hull. If the room is the point, a river will disappoint.

items.head: The reluctant socialiser
items.body: The same hundred guests all week is either a feature or a trial. Be honest about which.

title: Three who won't return to ocean

items.head: The town-centre walker
items.body: Once you've walked off into Budapest after dinner, a berth two miles out feels like a tax.

items.head: The one-good-table diner
items.body: No booking game, no venue strategy. One kitchen, one room, every night of the week.

items.head: The unpackers
items.body: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest, and the suitcase never moves. That is hard to give up.

right.label: Choose ocean
items: The ship is half the holiday
You want range in one week

text: The format is the decision. The line and the ship come after it.
sub: Get river-or-ocean right and almost any well-run vessel will do. Get it wrong and the best ship on the water is still the wrong week.

title: Save this before you choose a format
body: Or tell me what the week is for — the destination or the ship — and I'll point you at one of the two.
